analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for regulators to block big corporate mergers that would raise prices or lower wages.
analysis.headline: A bill to force companies behind mega-mergers — deals over $5 billion — to prove the deals would not hurt competition never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and got no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the nation's merger law to make it much harder for large companies to buy their competitors. It lowered the bar for what counts as an illegal merger, made the merging companies — not the government — prove big deals would not harm competition, and targeted "monopsony" power, when one dominant buyer squeezes suppliers and pushes down workers' wages. It also created a new FTC office to track industry concentration and required companies to report for five years after settling a merger case on whether the promised benefits actually happened.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be consumers facing higher prices from consolidated industries, workers in labor markets dominated by one or a few large employers, and small businesses and startups trying to compete against giants. The bill's own findings say concentration "depresses wages" and makes it harder to start a business. The FTC and Justice Department would also gain sharper legal tools, and a new Competition Advocate would give consumers, small businesses, and employees a channel to report anticompetitive behavior.

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the standard for blocking a merger: instead of only stopping deals that 'substantially' lessen competition, regulators could stop any deal that harms competition by more than a trivial amount — covering mergers that lower quality, reduce choice, slow innovation, or exclude competitors, not just ones that raise prices.

Shifts the burden of proof onto the companies in big mergers — deals over $5 billion, or deals involving companies with over $100 billion in assets or sales — so they, rather than taxpayers, must show the deal will not harm competition.
Adds 'monopsony' — one dominant buyer — to the merger law, aimed at companies that use their size to force suppliers to accept unreasonably low prices and workers to accept unreasonably low wages.

Requires companies that settle a merger challenge with the FTC or Justice Department to report annually for five years on pricing, quality, and whether the cost savings and consumer benefits they promised actually materialized.

Creates an Office of the Competition Advocate inside the FTC to collect concentration data, publish public reports, and build processes for consumers, small businesses, and employees to report possible anticompetitive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and private-equity buyers pursuing mergers would bear the cost: a harder legal standard, the burden of proving their deals are harmless, and five years of post-settlement reporting. Taxpayers would fund the new FTC office and data center. The general public could pay in a second, subtler way if some genuinely efficient mergers that would have lowered costs get blocked or abandoned under the tougher rules.

drawbacks.text: The tougher standard could chill some efficient mergers that genuinely lower costs: 'materially lessen competition' is defined as anything more than trivial harm, and companies above the size thresholds would have to prove a negative — that a deal will not harm competition — before closing, which raises deal costs and legal risk even for deals that would help consumers.

The size thresholds create cliff effects: a $4.9 billion deal would face the old, weaker standard while a $5.1 billion deal would face the presumption of harm, giving companies an incentive to structure deals just under the line.

The bill adds ongoing compliance work — five years of annual reporting after any merger settlement — plus the cost of standing up and staffing a new FTC office and data center, expenses that ultimately come out of company budgets and federal spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — a real check on corporate consolidation, protection for workers against monopsony wage pressure, and actual verification of companies' merger promises — weigh heavier than its costs, which are compliance burdens on merging companies and some risk of blocking efficient deals. It was a moderate proposal by antitrust standards, keeping enforcement within the existing agencies rather than creating new powers. But none of this was tested: the bill died in committee without a hearing, so neither the benefits nor the costs ever arrived.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in September 2017, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on September 14, 2017, joined by three Democratic cosponsors — Senators Gillibrand, Blumenthal, and Markey — as an original cosponsor list.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, the standard first step.

That was the last action of any kind: the bill sat in the Judiciary Committee for the rest of the 115th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies pursuing mergers — and the industries already consolidated around them — are better off, because no tougher merger standard ever arrived. The status quo, where the government must prove a merger is harmful and most big deals are approved, stayed in place.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MN), bill sponsor and senior Judiciary Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through the 115th Congress.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee hearing or markup on the bill, which then expired in committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on September 14, 2017 and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all four sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee never acted, so the bill never revealed whether it had broader support.

industries.industry: Large corporations in consolidated industries (tech, telecom, hospitals, agriculture, retail)
industries.note: The bill targets exactly these companies: any merger over $5 billion, or involving firms with $100 billion in assets or sales, would carry a presumption of harm unless the companies proved otherwise. Fewer approved mergers means fewer chances to buy competitors, raise prices, and squeeze suppliers and workers — which is why the bill's fate mattered more to them than to the public.

The bill's findings cite over $10 trillion in U.S. mergers and acquisitions since 2008, the deal flow this industry lives on. A burden-of-proof reversal and a lower harm standard would have made big deals riskier and slower to close, cutting into deal volume and fees.

industries.industry: Antitrust enforcement agencies (FTC and Justice Department)
industries.note: The bill would have handed both agencies a stronger legal standard, a reversed burden of proof in large mergers, five years of mandatory post-settlement data from merging companies, and a new Office of the Competition Advocate inside the FTC.

industries.industry: Small businesses, suppliers, and workers in concentrated labor markets
industries.note: The bill explicitly names monopsony power — one dominant buyer forcing suppliers to accept unreasonably low prices and workers to accept unreasonably low wages — as a merger harm, giving these groups a legal hook they largely lacked before.
